title: Indian Families Sold 50 Tonnes of Gold Last Quarter. It’s the Biggest Sell-Off in Years.
excerpt: Fearing prices could crater to ₹1.2 lakh per 10 grams, households are ditching heirloom jewellery for cold, hard cash — and India’s gold recycling industry is booming.
body:
Indian households have broken with a centuries-old tradition of hoarding gold, selling off nearly 50 tonnes of old jewellery, coins, and bars during the April-June quarter of 2026. That is a staggering 43 per cent jump compared to the same period last year, according to data from the India Bullion & Jewellers Association (IBJA) — one of the sharpest spikes in household gold recycling in recent memory.

The trigger is straightforward: fear. Earlier this year, domestic gold prices hit an all-time high of roughly ₹1.8 lakh per 10 grams on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX), with an intraday peak of ₹1,92,991. But a sustained correction has since dragged prices down to around ₹1.42 lakh. With market speculation mounting that prices could fall further — potentially to ₹1.2 lakh — consumers are rushing to lock in their gains while they still can.

“Indian consumers are leveraging the high price of gold for liquid cash,” said Surendra Mehta, National Secretary of the IBJA. “Though prices have fallen from a high of ₹1.8 lakh per 10 grams to ₹1.4 lakh, there is a fear among them that prices may further crash to ₹1.2 lakh, which is prompting them to sell gold to encash.”

International gold prices are heading for their biggest monthly decline since October 2008, with a drop of about 12.5 per cent in June alone. Comex gold futures have slipped below the $4,000 per ounce mark — their lowest in nearly eight months — before recovering to around $4,040.

## A Windfall for the Recycling Industry

The sell-off has been an unexpected windfall for India’s organised gold recycling sector. Muthoot Exim, the precious metals arm of the Muthoot Pappachan Group, reported a 40 per cent surge in old gold volumes across its national network of more than 100 Gold Point centres. The company buys used jewellery from consumers, refines it into 24-carat gold, and supplies the purified metal to manufacturers.

“Consumers are becoming more comfortable monetising idle gold through organised and transparent channels,” said Keyur Shah, CEO of Muthoot Exim. “This not only helps them unlock value but also supports the domestic gold ecosystem by bringing precious metal back into circulation.”

Augmont, another major player, has expanded its Gold For All network to 114 centres across multiple states. Director Ketan Kothari noted that India possesses one of the world’s largest household gold reserves, but much of it remains unused.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

Indian households collectively sit on an estimated 30,000 tonnes of gold — worth roughly $5 trillion according to a Kotak Institutional Equities research report from March, with the precious metal making up about 65 per cent of their non-property wealth. India imported gold worth $72.4 billion during FY26, making bullion one of the country’s largest import items.

In 2025, recycled gold contributed an estimated 125 to 150 tonnes to the Indian market. If the current trend continues, industry executives project recycled volumes could hit 200 to 250 tonnes by year-end — a meaningful rise that could slightly ease India’s heavy dependence on imported bullion.

But perspective matters. Even 50 tonnes is a rounding error against a 30,000-tonne stockpile. The question is whether this sell-off represents a temporary correction-driven reflex or a deeper structural shift in how Indian consumers view gold.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the gold sell-off has multiple dimensions. Many overseas Indians hold family gold back home — heirloom pieces passed down through generations. The sharp price correction may prompt conversations with family in India about whether to hold or sell, especially as gold’s role shifts from untouchable cultural asset to actively managed financial instrument.

The broader trend also raises questions about gold-backed lending. A parallel surge in households pledging jewellery as loan collateral suggests that for some families, the motivation is not opportunism but genuine need for liquidity.

For now, the message from India’s middle class is clear: when prices peak and the market turns, tradition takes a back seat to cash.
